Tuesday. Dilnaz's baking videos had eight thousand followers, and one of them, a user called Nitin_Truth, had commented on every post for a month: "Fake oven." "Nobody eats this." "Talentless." Tonight she spent an hour writing a clever reply. Her tea went cold.

Thursday. She read her reply again and deleted it. He wanted exactly this, her attention. She muted him, then blocked him. Her thumb shook a little, but it felt like shutting a noisy window.

Sunday. A new comment arrived from someone else: "Your sponge sank in the middle, like mine. Too much baking powder?" Dilnaz watched the clip again. The commenter was right.

She replied warmly, thanked them, and filmed a short fix for the next video. It got more likes than anything she'd posted. She didn't think about Nitin_Truth once that day.

qa.q: What did Nitin_Truth comment on Dilnaz's posts?
qa.a: "Fake oven." "Nobody eats this." "Talentless."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz feel when she muted and blocked the troll?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her thumb shaking a little, but also relieved, like shutting a noisy window.

qa.q: Which choice worked better for Dilnaz, and why?
qa.a: Ignoring the troll and engaging with the good-faith comment about the sponge, because it gave her useful help instead of feeding someone who only wanted a reaction.

qa.q: How might the commenter about the sunken sponge see Dilnaz's reply?
qa.a: They would likely feel appreciated and heard, since Dilnaz thanked them and even filmed a fix based on their tip.

grounding: Across several days, the passage shows someone learning to mute and block a troll who only wants a reaction while engaging with a good-faith critic.

"Disha, you keep refreshing that comment. Stop a minute. Your old uncle has a story.

Back when the internet was new, I, Samir, was twenty-three and wrote match reports for a cricket forum. There was one fellow, called himself Bouncer99. Every report, he'd write that I knew nothing, that my English was a joke. I stayed up nights writing long replies. He loved it. He'd come back with ten more.

Then a senior member messaged me: 'He's hungry. Stop feeding him.'

So I stopped. Didn't reply. Used the ignore button. Took a week before my fingers stopped itching.

Meanwhile a schoolteacher from Kanpur wrote that I'd got a scorecard wrong. I checked; she was right. I thanked her, fixed it, and we wrote to each other for years.

Ignore the hungry ones, beta. Answer the ones who actually want to talk."

qa.q: What was the name of the forum troll?
qa.a: Bouncer99.

qa.q: How did young Samir feel during the week after he stopped replying?
qa.a: He felt restless and itchy to reply, even though he knew answering only fed the troll.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Taking the senior member's advice to stop replying and use the ignore button, while still thanking the teacher who fixed a real mistake.

qa.q: How might the schoolteacher from Kanpur have seen Samir's response?
qa.a: She likely felt respected, since he thanked her and fixed the error, which led to years of friendly letters.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to ignore a troll who wanted a reaction while engaging warmly with a good-faith critic.

"When Shreya's video went viral, I'm Ishita, her roommate from college, and I just remember how she went quiet. Not crying. Quiet.

The comments were horrible. Hundreds of strangers about her face, her accent. Our friends were all posting public defences, arguing with trolls under her post. Which made it bigger.

I didn't know what to do, so I messaged her privately. Just: 'I'm here. What would help right now? You don't have to answer.'

She wrote back two hours later: 'Can you read my messages for me? I can't look.'

So I did. Every night for a week I went through her inbox, deleted the vile ones, saved the threatening ones for reporting, and sent her only the kind notes.

I didn't give her a list of advice. I just stayed. She told me later that was the thing that kept her standing."

qa.a: To read her messages for her, because she couldn't look.

qa.a: Shreya saw Ishita's steady presence as the thing that kept her standing during the trolling.

He wanted to jump in and argue with every one. Instead he sent her a private text: "Saw it. I'm so sorry. Do you want me to do anything, or just be around?"

Wednesday. Manjula hadn't posted in two days. She called him, voice thin. "I keep reading them. I can't stop." Thomas asked, "Want me to go through them for you? I'll save anything threatening and you don't have to see the rest."

"Yes. Please."

Saturday. He'd sorted it all. Two threats were reported. The rest he just deleted. He took her for dosa and didn't bring up the comments once.

She laughed for the first time that week. "You didn't lecture me," she said. "I noticed."

By Tuesday, her comments were full of anger. The potter's nephew had shared it, writing, "My uncle has worked forty years. This is what she thinks of us."

Her first instinct was to write that people had no sense of humour. Bhavna, her cousin, stopped her. "Would you say that to his face?"

Zainab watched her own video again. It was ugly. Her face burned.

On Sunday she went to the haat and found the potter. "I made fun of your work and your speech. It was wrong. I'm sorry." He looked at her a long moment and nodded.

She posted a plain apology, took the video down, and filmed him at his wheel the next week, asking him to explain his craft.

Bao had posted a quick review of a new noodle shop in Vancouver: "Great broth, shame the staff can barely speak English lol." He forgot about it by lunch.

By evening the shop's page had shared it with a reply from the owner's daughter, Chen: "My parents have worked twelve-hour days for thirty years. Their English is their third language."

Bao's stomach turned. His first thought was, It was a joke. His second was that his own grandmother had once been laughed at in a shop, and he had never forgotten her face.

He didn't delete and disappear. He wrote to Chen directly: "I was careless and unkind. I'm truly sorry to you and your parents. I'd like to apologise to them in person, if they're willing."

He went the next afternoon. The father listened, then set down a bowl in front of him. Bao ate, and the next week he edited his review to say only what it should have: great broth.

qa.a: "Shame the staff can barely speak English lol."

I'm Irfan, and I almost started a riot in my own family chat. That's how it felt, anyway.

Last Ramzan, my Khalu forwarded a video of men setting fire to a shop, with a caption saying it had happened in our town that morning. My hands went cold. My cousin Pooja lived two streets from the market. I had my thumb on Forward to my college group.

Then I noticed the shop signs weren't in any language I knew. And no local news had it. I did a reverse image search. The clip was from a different country, two years earlier.

I called Pooja. She was fine, eating iftar.

What stays with me is how strong the feeling was. The fear itself should have been my warning.

I messaged Khalu privately with the link. He was embarrassed at first. Now he sends me things before forwarding them. I count that as a win.

The staff room at the Lucknow coaching institute was buzzing. A clip was going round of the director, in his office, announcing that Monday's mock test was cancelled.

Varun, a young maths tutor, had already forwarded it to his batch of sixty students.

Rashmi, from the admin desk, frowned at her screen. "Varun, play it again. Watch his mouth."

He did. The words and the lips were slightly out of step. The director blinked oddly, almost never.

"And he never records videos," Rashmi said. "He hates cameras."

She checked the institute's official notice board online. Nothing. She called the director's office. The test was on.

Varun felt heat flood his face. "I look like an idiot."

"You look like someone who got tricked by a good fake," Rashmi said. "Someone made it to be believed."

He sent a correction to his batch, with the official notice attached, and asked them to delete the clip.

qa.a: Sixty students.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling after learning the clip was fake?

qa.q: What clues and checks exposed the fake clip?

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Varun's mistake?

Dear Chandrika Mausi,

I owe you an apology. Last week I forwarded you that video of the heart doctor from the television saying a spice mixture could replace blood pressure tablets. You asked me if it was real, and I said yes, because it looked exactly like him.

It wasn't him. My friend who works at a news site showed me: his mouth didn't match the words, his eyes hardly blinked, and his real hospital had posted a warning that someone had faked his face and voice. No proper news channel had ever reported it.

I felt so stupid, Mausi, and scared you might have stopped your tablets. Please don't. If you have questions, let's ask your doctor together on Thursday.

My friend said something that helped: a fake like that is built to fool careful people. That's its whole job.

I'll check before I send you anything now.

Love,
Arohi

Jatin was stuck at the airport in Kolkata, his flight cancelled, when the message came from an unknown number: a photo of him, face clear, in a hotel room he had never been in, with a woman he had never met. "Pay 50,000 by tonight or this goes to your office and family."

His knees went weak. It was fake; he knew it was fake. But it looked real.

He called Jagdish, his older brother, from a corner of the departure hall. "I haven't done anything. I swear."

"I believe you," Jagdish said at once. "Listen. Don't pay. Don't reply. Take screenshots of everything, the number, the photo, the message."

"And then?"

"Report it on the cybercrime portal right now, from your phone. I'll call my friend who's a lawyer. And I'll tell Maa before anyone else can."

Jatin sat on the cold floor, filling in the form, hands shaking. It was not his shame, Jagdish kept saying. It was someone else's crime.

What did Jatin feel when he saw the fake photo?
qa.a: He felt panicked and ashamed, his knees going weak, even though he knew it was fake.

qa.q: Which of Jagdish's steps protected Jatin, and why?
qa.a: Refusing to pay, saving screenshots, reporting on the cybercrime portal, calling a lawyer and telling their mother first, which kept evidence and took away the blackmailer's power.

qa.a: Jagdish sees it as someone else's crime and a violation, not Jatin's shame, and believes his brother at once.

Two days before the panchayat vote in Rampur, a voice note went round the village: if Shreya's panel won, the water tanker would stop coming to the lower mohalla. Hafsa's mother heard it at the handpump and came home pale.

"Ammi, who sent it?" Hafsa asked.

"Everyone has it."

Hafsa listened twice. The voice was a stranger's. No name, no date. She thought: who gains if the lower mohalla is scared?

In the evening she walked to the panchayat office and asked the clerk. The tanker was paid for by the district, not by any panel. She also found Shreya at a tea stall and asked her straight. Shreya laughed tiredly. "I've heard it too. It's not true. Come to the meeting tomorrow."

Hafsa went to the meeting and to the other panel's meeting as well. Then she told her mother, and the women at the handpump, what she'd found.

In the hospital canteen, Anand pushed his phone across the table to Lalit. "Read this. The new ration cards have tracking chips in them. They're watching where we go."

Lalit's first impulse was to laugh. He'd worked with Anand for three years; Anand was the best nurse on the ward. Laughing would crush him.

"How did you come across it?" Lalit asked.

"My cousin sent it. And my neighbour's card got cut off after she moved. That's proof, isn't it?"

Lalit nodded slowly. "That sounds really stressful for her. Here's one thing I know: my sister works at the ration office. The cards don't have chips. They have a printed code, like a barcode. Cut-offs usually happen when the address isn't updated."

Anand frowned. "Your sister's sure?"

"I'll ask her to show you one tomorrow. You can look for yourself."

Anand picked his phone back up, quieter now. "Okay. I'll look."

qa.q: Where does Lalit's sister work?
qa.a: At the ration office.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when Anand first showed him the post?
qa.a: He felt an urge to laugh but also protective and fond of Anand, not wanting to humiliate him.

qa.q: Which part of Lalit's approach made Anand willing to listen?
qa.a: Asking how Anand came across it, sharing one reliable fact from his sister, and offering a chance to see a card, without mocking him.

Dear Abhinav,

I've been thinking about Saturday's dinner, and I owe you a better conversation than the one I gave you.

When you said the old fort was built by aliens because no one could have lifted those stones, I laughed. Then I pulled up articles on my phone and read them out to the whole table like a lawyer. Vijay

Tanvir's diary, Friday, very late

I made a mess today and I need to write it out.

This morning I shared a message in our colony group: a child kidnapper had been seen near the school, a vegetable vendor with a blue cart. I didn't check. I was scared for my niece.

By noon, parents had surrounded Ujjwal-bhaiya, the man who sells vegetables from a blue cart, shouting. Someone pushed him. The police came and said there was no such report anywhere. The message was months old, from another state.

I felt sick. I deleted my post. Then I wrote a correction in the same group, in capitals: FALSE. MY MISTAKE. PLEASE DON'T FORWARD.

In the evening I went to Ujjwal-bhaiya's cart. I said sorry, by name, in front of the neighbours. He was quiet, then said, "Just check next time."

I will. Shame isn't enough. I need the habit.

qa.q: What did the false message say about the kidnapper?
qa.a: That a vegetable vendor with a blue cart had been seen near the school.

qa.q: What did Tanvir feel after the police said there was no such report?
qa.a: Tanvir felt sick with guilt and shame for sharing a false message that led to Ujjwal-bhaiya being pushed.

qa.q: What steps did Tanvir take to repair the harm?
qa.a: Tanvir deleted the post, posted a clear correction to the same group, and apologised to Ujjwal-bhaiya by name in front of the neighbours.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal-bhaiya see the apology?
qa.a: Ujjwal-bhaiya may feel hurt but somewhat respected, accepting it quietly while asking Tanvir to check next time.

grounding: The diary shows someone who shared something false that caused panic and hurt a named person, deleting it, correcting it to the same audience and apologising, and committing to check first.

Soo-ah noticed it on a Sunday in Seoul: she had been scrolling for three hours, and she was furious. About a celebrity scandal. About a stranger's opinion on buses. About things that had nothing to do with her life.

Her friend Rafael had texted twice. She hadn't answered.

That evening she met him at the noodle stall. "You look angry," he said.

"I am. I don't even know at what."

"Your feed?"

She laughed, embarrassed. "My feed."

On the walk home she made a plan. She unfollowed ten accounts that only made her angry. She followed two long-form science writers and her local library. She set a rule: no phone after nine, and a paper book on the pillow instead.

Two weeks later she noticed she was sleeping better, and she'd stopped thinking everyone on the bus was an idiot. Rafael noticed too. "You're back," he said.

qa.q: How many accounts did Soo-ah unfollow?
qa.a: Ten accounts.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling after three hours of scrolling?

passage:
In the working women's hostel in Bengaluru, lights-out was at eleven, but Tenzin's phone glowed under the blanket till two. Videos about politics, then angrier videos, then comments on the videos. She woke up tired and snapped at the canteen staff over cold idli.

Her roommate Kalyani caught her at breakfast. "You've been different. Short with everyone."

Tenzin wanted to argue, then didn't. "I think it's the phone. It shows me whatever makes me angriest."

"So choose what it shows you."

That week Tenzin deleted the video app for a month. She joined the hostel reading circle on Wednesdays and started a thick novel from the library. She kept one news site she trusted and read it once a day, at lunch.

By the end of the month, she apologised to the canteen staff, and Kalyani found her asleep before eleven, book open on her chest.

qa.q: Until what time did Tenzin's phone glow under the blanket?
qa.a: Till two.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel in the mornings after late-night scrolling?
qa.a: She felt tired and irritable, snapping at the canteen staff.

qa.q: What small steps helped Tenzin change her habits?
qa.a: Deleting the video app for a month, joining the reading circle, reading a novel and limiting news to one trusted site once a day.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Tenzin's behaviour at first?
qa.a: Kalyani notices she has become short with everyone and is concerned enough to say so kindly.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose feed keeps her angry and hooked, affecting her mood, who curates sources, reads long-form and schedules offline time.
